title: Tic-Tac-Toe
description: Online game-state class. After each `play`, check only the four lines that pass through that cell — row, column, and (if on a diagonal) the two diagonals. O(n) per move instead of scanning the whole board.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Design a TicTacToe class for an n×n board. `play(player, row, col)` records a move and returns the winner ('X' or 'O') if this move wins, else ''. Quick clarifications:"

• Are moves guaranteed valid — never on an occupied cell, never out of bounds?
• Player tokens — always 'X' and 'O', or arbitrary strings?
• Does `play` need to handle a turn order, or can the same player play twice (assume caller alternates)?
• Once someone wins, can `play` still be called? What should it return — '' or the prior winner?
• Is `n` always 3 or arbitrary? (Affects whether the diagonal-cells short-circuit matters.)
sections.why: The arbitrary-n question is what unlocks the elegant tally-based solution. If n were always 3 you could hardcode 8 lines and be done. For arbitrary n, you need the +1/-1 tally per row/col/diagonal trick — that's the whole reason this problem exists in interview rotation. Asking the question up front signals you saw the generalization.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n²) per move solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: maintain the full board as a 2D array. After each `play`, scan the row, column, and (if on a diagonal) the two diagonals, checking if all n cells match the just-played player. That's O(n) per line × up to 4 lines = O(n) per move. Not bad, but it does the work proportional to the board size on every move.

We can do better: instead of re-scanning the cells, maintain a TALLY per line — increment by +1 when X plays in it, decrement by -1 when O plays. A line's tally equals n when X has filled it, -n when O has, anything in between means it's mixed or partial. That's O(1) per move."
sections.why: Naming the O(n) board-scan first proves you understand the basic structure. The pivot to tallies is non-obvious — it relies on the trick that 'sum of integers' is a constant-time aggregate, and that fixed sign reservation per player makes 'sum equals ±n' a clean win signal. Walking through this derivation out loud is what gets credit.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: Why does a +1/-1 tally per line work?
sections.say:
"The insight is: a line wins if and only if it's filled with exactly one player's tokens. Equivalently: if I assign +1 to X and -1 to O, the line wins iff the sum is +n (all X) or -n (all O). Any mix of X and O on the line gives a sum strictly between -n and +n in absolute value.

With 4 line types — rows, cols, main diagonal, anti-diagonal — each cell (r, c) belongs to:
• row r (always)
• col c (always)
• main diag (only if r === c)
• anti diag (only if r + c === n - 1)

So each move updates AT MOST 4 tallies — O(1) regardless of n. After the update, check if any of those 4 hit ±n; if so, return the player. O(n) space for the row and col tally arrays.

The diagonal conditions are the load-bearing arithmetic: main diag = top-left to bottom-right means row index equals col index. Anti-diag = top-right to bottom-left means r + c is constant — specifically `n - 1` (the corner (0, n-1) and (n-1, 0) both satisfy it)."
sections.why: Naming the +n/-n math is the differentiator. Most candidates remember 'use tallies' but blank on why ±n is the win threshold or where the diagonal conditions come from. Deriving `r + c === n - 1` from 'the anti-diagonal passes through (0, n-1) and (n-1, 0)' shows you can rebuild the formula, not just memorize it.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three games on a 3×3 board — X wins the main diagonal, O wins the top row, and X wins the anti-diagonal. Each trace shows the tally fields after each move and the per-move return value."

examples.note: X completes the main diagonal (0,0)-(1,1)-(2,2). diag tally hits +3.
examples.trace:
init: rows=[0,0,0] cols=[0,0,0] diag=0 anti=0
X(0,0) v=+1: rows[0]=1 cols[0]=1 r===c→diag=1 r+c=0≠2 (no anti). |tallies|<3 → ''
O(0,1) v=-1: rows[0]=0 cols[1]=-1 r≠c r+c=1≠2. → ''
X(1,1) v=+1: rows[1]=1 cols[1]=0 r===c→diag=2 r+c=2→anti=1. → ''
O(0,2) v=-1: rows[0]=-1 cols[2]=-1 r≠c r+c=2→anti=0. → ''
X(2,2) v=+1: rows[2]=1 cols[2]=0 r===c→diag=3 r+c=4≠2. |diag|=3=n → return 'X'

examples.note: O sweeps the top row. row[0] tally hits -3.
X completes the anti-diagonal (0,2)-(1,1)-(2,0). anti tally hits +3.

sections.why: The three traces collectively confirm all 4 win-detection lines fire (row, col x2 implicitly, diag, anti-diag). The anti-diag trace is the most error-prone — easy to write `r + c === n` (off by one) instead of `r + c === n - 1`. Tracing (0,2)+(1,1)+(2,0) on n=3 confirms the formula: 0+2=2, 1+1=2, 2+0=2, all equal n-1=2. ✓

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me walk through edges:
• **Full board draw** — no line ever sums to ±n. Final `play` returns ''. Caller is responsible for detecting 'all cells used' to declare a draw; this class only signals winners.
• **Move played on an already-occupied cell** — the spec says assume valid input, but if violated, the tally double-counts and you could falsely declare a win with fewer than n unique cells. In a defensive variant I'd guard with a Set of played cells.
• **Instant win on first move** — impossible. Smallest n is 3, smallest line is 3 cells, so a player needs at least 3 plays to win. The first 2 plays always return ''. Worth stating because interviewers love impossibility proofs.
• **n = 1** — degenerate. The single cell is row 0, col 0, AND on both diagonals. One play wins. The tallies fire 4 times simultaneously, all 4 if-checks would return — but the first hit short-circuits. Fine.
• **Cell on both diagonals** — only the center cell of an odd-n board satisfies both `r === c` AND `r + c === n - 1`. The two if-statements (not else-if) both fire, updating both `diag` and `anti`. Correct behavior — that move legitimately participates in both diagonals.
• **Off-board move** — `rows[row]` with `row >= n` would throw or silently extend the array. Defensive guard if not promised valid."
sections.why: The 'instant win impossible' beat is the cute pre-condition that shows you've thought about the move sequence, not just the algorithm. The 'both diagonals at center' beat is the gotcha that catches careless `else if` use — if you write `if (r === c) ... else if (r + c === n - 1) ...`, the center cell only updates `diag`, missing `anti`. Using two separate `if`s (not else-if) is what saves it.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(1) per `play` — exactly 4 tally updates, 4 absolute-value comparisons. No loops over board cells. Strictly constant regardless of n.

Space is O(n) — two arrays of length n (rows and cols), plus two scalars (diag, anti). For n = 3, that's 8 numbers total.

Compared to the naive 'scan after each move' approach: that's O(n) per play because each line has n cells to check. So the tally trick is the difference between O(1) and O(n) per move. For a long game (e.g., a streamed series of moves where many never trigger a win), the tally version is dramatically cheaper.

The template generalizes to any 'check N-in-a-line with incremental updates' problem — Connect Four if N were small enough to fit in a fixed counter, or game-state problems where moves can only ADD to the state (no undos). The +1/-1 trick specifically works when there are exactly two players or two states; for k > 2 players you'd switch to a hash of `(line → counts per player)`."
sections.why: The O(1) vs O(n) per-move framing is the headline. The 'two players is what makes +1/-1 work' caveat is the extension — interviewers sometimes ask 'what if there were 3 players?' and the right answer is 'I'd use a count Map per line instead of a single integer tally', not 'I'd use ±1, ±2 sentinels' (which doesn't generalize because 1+2 = 3 = -3 mod something is ambiguous).

walkthrough.intro: Step through a sequence of TicTacToe plays. Watch the per-row, per-col, and diagonal tallies evolve (+1 for X, -1 for O). Each play()'s return is collected into a results array; |tally| === n signals a win for that line.

n=3 — O wins top row in 6 moves
n=3 — X wins anti-diagonal in 5 moves

trace: yield { line: 2, label: `new TicTacToe(${n}) — rows=[0,0,0], cols=[0,0,0], diag=0, anti=0`, state: { n, rowsT: [...rowsT], colsT: [...colsT], diag, anti, results: [...results] } };
yield { line: 11, label: `move#${k}: play('${player}', ${row}, ${col}) → v=${v}`, state: { n, rowsT: [...rowsT], colsT: [...colsT], diag, anti, player, row, col, v, results: [...results] } };
yield { line: 13, label: `rows[${row}] → ${rowsT[row]}, cols[${col}] → ${colsT[col]}`, state: { n, rowsT: [...rowsT], colsT: [...colsT], diag, anti, player, row, col, results: [...results] } };
yield { line: 15, label: `(${row},${col}) on main diag → diag = ${diag}`, state: { n, rowsT: [...rowsT], colsT: [...colsT], diag, anti, player, row, col, results: [...results] } };

yield { line: 17, label: `(${row},${col}) on anti diag (row+col=${row + col}=${n - 1}) → anti = ${anti}`, state: { n, rowsT: [...rowsT], colsT: [...colsT], diag, anti, player, row, col, results: [...results] } };
yield { line: 23, label: `check |tally|===${n}? → return '${winRet}'`, state: { n, rowsT: [...rowsT], colsT: [...colsT], diag, anti, results: [...results], returnedThisMove: winRet } };

yield { line: 23, label: `all moves processed — results=${JSON.stringify(results)}`, state: { n, rowsT: [...rowsT], colsT: [...colsT], diag, anti, results: [...results], returns: JSON.stringify(results) } };

notes: Tally per line (+1 for X, -1 for O). |tally| === n is a win — sign tells you which player.
Diagonals: main has `row === col`; anti-diagonal has `row + col === n - 1`.
O(1) per move with O(n) space — beats the naive 'scan the whole board' check on every move.

alternates.label: Board-scan after each move (O(n) per move)
alternates.when: Reach for this when n is small and fixed (classic 3×3), or when you want the simplest possible code before optimizing. The board representation is more readable; the tally trick is the optimization you add once correctness is proven.
notes: Board is an n×n array; each play() scans up to 4 lines of n cells — O(n) vs O(1) for tallies.
Short-circuit the diagonal scans with the same `row === col` / `row + col === n - 1` guards — otherwise you'd scan the full main diag on every non-diagonal move.
Uses O(n²) space instead of O(n); upgrade to tallies once correctness is confirmed.

questions.q: Why use +1 / -1 tallies instead of scanning the board after each move?
options: Tallies can be packed into a single 32-bit integer, while a 2D board requires `n²` allocations
Each move only touches up to 4 lines — O(1) per move vs O(n²) for a scan
The board scan can't detect diagonal wins because adjacent diagonal cells aren't contiguous in memory
Tallies generalize to k > 2 players via additional sentinel values, which a board scan cannot

questions.q: What condition signals that `(row, col)` lies on the anti-diagonal of an n×n board?
options: row === col — the anti-diagonal mirrors the main diagonal so the same identity holds
row === n - col — the diagonal passes through (1, n-1) and (n-1, 1)
(row + 1) * (col + 1) === n — derived from the corner product invariant
`Math.abs` normalizes the tally back to a non-negative range so it can be safely used as an array index in the next move
X is +n on a win, O is -n — absolute value detects either
Negative tallies would otherwise satisfy the `=== n` check via sign coercion in `===`
Tallies can wrap past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` on long games; abs collapses the overflow

questions.q: What does `play` return when the move does NOT end the game?
options: null — the absence of a winner is signaled by the absence of a value
false — `play` returns a boolean indicating whether the game continues
The current player's token — so the caller knows whose move it was, but without a win flag

exercises.prompt: Fill in TicTacToe so X wins down the diagonal; non-wins log 'no'.

L3.prompt: Implement TicTacToe(n) with play(player, row, col). Play 5 moves where X wins the main diagonal; log 'no' for non-wins and the winner string for the final move.
hints: Track per-row, per-col, and the two diagonal tallies — add +1 for X, -1 for O.
Main diagonal cells satisfy `row === col`; anti-diagonal `row + col === n - 1`.
Return `player` when any tally hits ±n, else ''.
